LIVE_APP_TEXT: all 44 alerts named an app: the attacking process in 43, and an unrelated app that APP-001 flagged in one.
LIVE_MISS_TEXT: Frozen version 1.5.0 detected 27, raising no alert for failed lookups, which needs answers from the lab's DNS server. The laptop has two adapters on the network, so that server's answers could leave from an address the phone would reject. Once it answered from the address asked, the scenario fired in 10 of 10 runs, though we cannot show that this caused the miss.
IDLE_TEXT: Quiet connections separate the relays. We opened a TCP connection through each tool, stayed silent, then sent a line and waited for its echo. With no capture and through version 1.5.1 the connection survives 300~s of silence, and 600~s on the emulator. Through version 1.5.0 and PCAPdroid, which also relays with zdtun, it is dead by 90~s, and an app holding one open for push messages has to reconnect.
IDENTITY_TEXT: We ran frozen version 1.5.0 with app identity switched off, so that detectors count per source address as a network sensor must, over two consecutive 13-minute sessions on the same sites and apps. With identity on, the live session raised no alerts over 139{,}506 packets. Replaying those same packets without identity raised one, and the live session with identity off raised two over 98{,}403 packets, all of them the horizontal scan rule reading page loads as a scan. Of the 28 attack scenarios, version 1.5.1 detected 27 with identity off, losing only the TLS library change, which needs identity by definition. These counts are small and bound the claim: on this traffic identity spares a few false alarms and changes no other detection. Beyond that, an alert with identity names the app to remove, where without it every alert names the phone's address.
ABSTRACT_IDENTITY: Switching app identity off adds two false alarms in a session and stops alerts naming the app.
SPEED_TEXT: The relay is no longer what limits the phone. With the full app in the background it moves 160~Mbit/s down and 173 up, over three times version 1.4.0's 39 and 47, and level with PCAPdroid given the link, since single transfers with no capture ranged from 110 to 200~Mbit/s. The analysis queue skipped no packets in any round. What this costs is processor and memory, 66\% of a core and 311~MiB against PCAPdroid's 19\% and 151~MiB, and it buys detection that PCAPdroid's free build does not run.
ABSTRACT_SPEED: Through the full pipeline the phone moves 160~Mbit/s down and 173 up, level with PCAPdroid, and keeps quiet connections that PCAPdroid drops, at the cost of more CPU and memory.
CONCLUSION_SPEED: Its relay keeps pace with PCAPdroid's and holds quiet connections that PCAPdroid drops, while using more CPU and memory.
SAMSUNG_HARDWARE: A second unrooted phone, a mid-range Samsung Galaxy M53 (MediaTek MT6877, 6~GB RAM, Android~16), ran the live scenarios, a browsing and app session, and shorter speed tests.
SAMSUNG_LIVE_TEXT: On the second phone, 28 did, and its browsing and app session raised no alerts over 179{,}730 packets.
SAMSUNG_SPEED_TEXT: The Samsung Galaxy M53 moved 86~Mbit/s down and 127 up through the full app over two rounds, against 122 and 131 with no capture.
SAMSUNG_COST_TEXT: With the scheduler free to choose its core, the Samsung Galaxy M53 sustains about 8{,}500.
LIMITS_TEXT: Limits were set on one phone, and a session on one other is thin evidence that they suit others
ENERGY_TEXT: Under the 10~Mbit/s download both apps' draw stays within the spread between repetitions of the no-capture baseline, with AndroNet's process at 21\% of a core against PCAPdroid's 5\%. At idle AndroNet adds 0.15~W, while PCAPdroid's draw stays within the spread.
SOAK_PHONES_NOTE: on the Pixel 8 and an entry-level Oppo A53
SOAK_TEXT: Two phones ran version 1.5.1 in their owners' everyday use, with profiles empty at the start and logging only each alert's time, finding and app: the Pixel~8, an author's own phone, and an entry-level Oppo A53 (Snapdragon~460, 4~GB RAM, Android~12). On the Pixel, capture ended after 11 hours, once the app had run for six: Android 15 and later allow a data-sync foreground service, the type version 1.5.1 declared, six hours of running time a day and crash an app that keeps one running longer. Version 1.5.2 declares a special-use service instead and changes nothing else; with the limit cut to five minutes, 1.5.1 crashed again and 1.5.2 kept its tunnel up for all eight minutes. On the Oppo, capture ran for 30 hours in one process, until the phone restarted to install a system update, with no crash or freeze recorded. They analysed 0.6 and 0.3~million packets with none skipped. The Pixel raised 16 alerts, about 34.6 a day, and the Oppo 21, about 17.0 a day, each naming an app: 16 from FLOW-003, 12 from the bulk upload rule and nine from APP-001. The Oppo's 16 FLOW-003 alerts all came from one app, about once an hour. No attack was staged, so we count every alert as a false alarm.
ABSTRACT_SOAK: In 41 hours of everyday use on two phones it raised 37 alerts and hit Android~15's six-hour daily cap on capture, now fixed.
